solda_t: Never soldered before? Read this before turning on the iron
solda_li:
• Practice first. Make about ten wire splices using scrap wire before touching the robot's parts. Wear safety glasses and solder in a well-ventilated area: the iron tip gets hotter than 300 °C.
  • Tin both parts. Melt a little solder onto the stripped wire and a little onto the terminal, separately. Then touch them together and heat them: they join in 2 or 3 seconds.
  • Heat the joint, not the solder. Touch the iron to the wire and terminal at the same time, and feed the solder to the hot joint, not to the iron tip.
  • A good solder joint is smooth and wraps around the wire. Dull, grainy, or ball-shaped solder is a cold joint: it makes poor contact. Heat it again until it flows.
  • Check with a multimeter. Set it to continuity mode, the one that beeps, and test each joint. Before putting the cells in the holder, check that the positive and negative terminals are not connected.
  • Never solder directly to an 18650 cell. Heat damages the cell, and it can leak or catch fire. On this robot, solder the battery connection to the holder's metal strip, with the cells out of the holder. Another option is to ask a battery shop for a pre-soldered pack with wires: in that case, first check that it fits where the holder goes.
  • Get help with the battery. If you are under 18 or don't feel safe, ask an adult or an electronics technician to do the battery soldering.

resumo: The capybara is a [[N_ALTURA]] cm robot for you to print at home and assemble. It rolls on two wheels hidden in its haunches and two support balls at the front, under its paws; its head turns 60° to each side and tilts; its mouth opens. Inside are a Raspberry Pi, an Arduino, three servos, two motors, and a battery that charges via USB-C. You need a 3D printer with a 256 mm build plate, the parts on the shopping list, and a soldering iron. This page covers phase 1: the assembled body, connected wires, and centred servos. Programming (walking, voice, camera, AI) is phase 2 and has not been done yet.

mon_sub: First, four workbench prep steps with the parts still loose: all the soldering happens here. Then assembly, in the same order the checker tested: each part goes in from the indicated side without hitting anything already assembled.
prep_p: These prep steps come first because it’s much easier to solder, measure, and adjust the loose parts on the workbench than inside the body. All soldering for the robot is done here; during assembly, you only use screw terminals and plug-in connections. Prep steps 1, 2, and 3 are electrical and have not been bench-tested: measure every connection with a multimeter before turning on the switch. The sequence matches the wiring file, step by step.
prep1_p: You assemble the wiring harness by following the wiring diagram, with the printed chassis beside you. Don’t connect the Raspberry Pi, Arduino, motor driver, or servos yet.
prep2_p: The program is the sketch centrar_servos.ino. It moves all 3 servos to the middle point and holds them there, with the motors off.
prep2_b: Don’t power the servos through USB: it supplies 0,5 A, and an MG996R servo needs more when starting up. Never connect the computer’s USB cable while the battery is on. To upload the program again later, pull out the Arduino tray.
prep3_p: The Raspberry Pi and Arduino sit in trays, one above the other. They communicate through 3 wires, and the Pi gets power through 4 wires on the pins. Here you prepare and label those cables, assemble the 3-resistor divider that protects the Pi from the Arduino’s 5 V, and set aside the motor driver wires. After this prep step, there’s no more soldering.
prep3_b: Where to find pin 1 and why the pin number is not the GPIO number: Raspberry Pi documentation. On a powered-on Pi, the pinout command draws the pin map. There is about 19 mm left above the Pi up to the top tray (measurement unconfirmed): bend the wires just above the connectors.
prep4_p: The card is flashed on your computer with a microSD card reader. Then you connect to the Raspberry Pi over the network using SSH: you type commands on your computer, and they run on the Pi.
prep4_b: Sources: Raspberry Pi documentation on GitHub (SSH and how to find the Pi's address). The serial line comes from the Raspberry Pi firmware overlay list; after restarting, the port name appears with ls /dev/ttyAMA*. Not bench-tested.
prep_nota: Threaded inserts: set the iron between 220 and 250 °C, a little above the printing temperature for the part's plastic (typical value, NC). Place the tip inside the insert, let the heat soften the plastic, and slowly push without forcing it until the insert is flush with the surface. If your iron has no temperature control, apply heat for less time.

mon_paraf_p: There are [[N_INSERTOS]] M3 heat-set inserts. Seat them all before you start assembling.

mon_abrir_p: Replacing the battery or working on the boards does not require removing the head: only the rear door comes off, with 2 screws.
en_sub: Two 18650 batteries in series provide 6 to 8.4 V. Three power lines come from them: 5.1 V for the Raspberry Pi, Arduino, and driver logic; 6 V for the servos; and battery voltage for the wheel motors.
seg_li:
• None of this has been bench-tested. The wiring diagram is based on the component datasheets. Check each connection with a multimeter before turning on the switch.
  • Polarity: red to positive, black to negative. Measure before each new connection. Reversed wires burn out the board immediately.
  • Adjust before connecting the load: set the LM2596 to 5.1 V and the UBEC to 6 V, measured with a multimeter, with the Raspberry Pi, Arduino, and servos disconnected.
  • A short circuit can start a fire: solder with the cells OUT of the holder and insulate each splice with heat-shrink tubing. The 3 A fuse goes right after the holder.
  • Matching cells: use two new 18650 cells from the same brand and model. Take dented, swollen, or hot cells to a battery collection point, not the robot.
  • First charge: stay nearby, with the robot on a surface that won’t burn.
en_f3: LM2596: 5.1 V for the boards · UBEC: 6 V for the servos · L298N: wheel motors
en1_t: 5,1 V for the Raspberry Pi and Arduino
en1_p: The LM2596 converter keeps the output at 5 V until the battery drops to about 6.5 V. Its output goes to a terminal block inside the body. From there, 4 jumpers go to the Raspberry Pi's 5 V and GND pins, one pair goes to the + and − pins of the Sensor Shield's COM connector, and one wire goes to the driver's +5V terminal. The board can handle about 2 A continuously without a heatsink (typical value, NC): use the Pi 4, or the Pi 5 without USB accessories. If the Pi reports undervoltage (the vcgencmd get_throttled command returns something other than throttled=0x0), shorten these wires and check the 5.1 V.
en2_p: The UBEC supplies 3 A continuously to the 3 servos through the Sensor Shield's blue screw terminal, with the SEL jumper removed. With the jumper in place, the 6 V would reach the Arduino's 5 V line. A 1000 µF capacitor on the screw terminal handles the startup surge. When all servos stall at once, they draw more than 3 A: the phase 2 program must stop them before they reach the end of their travel.
en3_p: The balanced charger stands upright inside the tail, with its opening facing down: the plug goes in under the tail. It accepts a USB-C power supply up to 15 W and needs a third wire soldered to the point joining the two cells. It connects before the switch, so the robot charges while switched off.
en4_t: Wheel motors and communication between the boards
en4_p: The L298N motor driver receives battery voltage and connects the 2 motors as directed by the Arduino, through 6 signal wires. The Raspberry Pi and Arduino communicate over a 3-wire serial connection (UART): the Pi transmits on pin 32 and receives on pin 33. These numbers are the pin positions in the row of 40, counted from the corner of the microSD card; they are not the GPIO numbers. The Arduino runs at 5 V and the Pi at 3.3 V: 3 1 kΩ resistors, attached to the terminal block, lower the voltage on the wire going from the Arduino to the Pi. On the Pi system, enable serial with one line in the configuration file: dtoverlay=uart5 on the Pi 4 or dtoverlay=uart4-pi5 on the Pi 5 (prep step 4).

en_nota: Currents calculated from the specifications, not measured. Normal use: about 2.5 A drawn from the battery pack, with the Raspberry Pi, servos, and wheels running. Peak: close to 8 A if the servos reach the UBEC limit and both motors stall at the same time. The KCD11-101 switch is rated for 3 A at 250 V~ and 6 A at 125 V~ (store specification), with no DC current rating. That is why the fuse is 3 A, the switch's lowest rated value, and slow-blow (marked T3A). This is the weak point in this electrical setup: normal use is close to the limit, and the fuse may blow when the robot works hard. If it blows, do not use a higher-rated fuse: the switch cannot handle it. The phase 2 program must ramp up the wheels and avoid forcing the head at the same time.
